Viscosity of motor oils (SAE)

plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four tall graduated cylinders arranged side by side on a common base labeled "Oil viscosity (SAE)," each filled with motor oil of a different SAE grade — 20, 30, 40, and 50 from left to right — and each holding a metal sphere dropped simultaneously from the top so that its position at a single elapsed moment reveals the oil's resistance to flow. The oils range progressively in color from pale yellow (SAE 20) to a deeper orange-red (SAE 50), and the position of the sphere descends less and less as the SAE grade increases: the sphere has fallen to the lower portion of the tube in grade 20, slightly higher in grade 30, noticeably higher in grade 40, and only to slightly above the midpoint of the column in grade 50. Because a more viscous fluid exerts a greater drag force on the sphere, slowing it to a lower terminal velocity, the shorter distance traveled in a fixed time directly encodes the ranking of viscosity across grades. The side-by-side format at a single instant converts viscosity — an intrinsic property — into a visually comparable positional difference, removing any need for stopwatches or calculations. This figure demonstrates viscosity as a rank-orderable physical property and establishes that higher SAE-grade oils offer greater internal resistance to the motion of an object moving through them.

elements: Flat rectangular wooden/amber base slab (platform) with visible top face and front edge, spanning the full width of the scene
Text label 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' printed on the front face / front strip of the base slab
Four identical tall graduated cylinders standing upright, evenly spaced left to right on the slab
Each cylinder: transparent pale blue-grey glass tube wall with thin outline
Each cylinder: flared conical pour spout/lip at the top, slightly wider than the tube
Each cylinder: hexagonal stepped glass foot/base at the bottom
Oil column inside each tube filling ~85% of the tube height, with a meniscus at the top surface
Oil color graded by SAE number: pale yellow (20), yellow (30), orange (40), orange-red (50), each with a vertical light-to-dark gradient
One polished steel sphere suspended inside each oil column, with specular highlight and soft shadow
Sphere heights differ: lowest in SAE 20, progressively higher in 30, 40, and highest in 50
Numeric grade labels '20', '30', '40', '50' on the slab top surface directly beneath each cylinder
Soft contact shadows of the cylinder feet on the slab

interactions.label: Drop all four spheres simultaneously
interactions.teaches: At a single elapsed instant, the sphere has fallen farthest in the thinnest oil and least in the thickest, so distance fallen ranks viscosity directly

interactions.label: Oil SAE grade (single-cylinder focus)
interactions.teaches: Viscosity varies continuously: raising the grade darkens the oil and smoothly slows one ball's steady descent

interactions.label: Show terminal velocity labels
interactions.teaches: Each sphere settles at a constant terminal speed inversely proportional to viscosity — the numbers behind the visual ranking
The cylinders are real 3D tubes on a slab; rotating confirms the spheres are inside the fluid columns, not drawn on a flat panel

demo_steps.title: The four oils at rest
demo_steps.narration: Four graduated cylinders hold motor oils of grade SAE 20, 30, 40 and 50, each darkening in color as the grade rises. A steel sphere waits at the top of each column.

demo_steps.title: Release all four at once
demo_steps.narration: Released together, the spheres separate almost immediately: the one in SAE 20 races down while the one in SAE 50 crawls. Distance fallen in the same time ranks the oils' resistance to flow.

demo_steps.title: Read the terminal speeds
demo_steps.narration: Each sphere quickly reaches a constant terminal velocity where drag balances weight. The labels show the speed falling as viscosity climbs from grade 20 to 50.

demo_steps.title: Sweep one cylinder through the grades
demo_steps.narration: Focusing on a single tube and sliding the grade from 20 to 50 shows the change is continuous — the oil deepens toward orange-red and the ball's steady descent slows smoothly.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: base slab 10 x 0.45 x 2.6 world units (X = screen-right width, Y = slab thickness, Z = depth), top face at y = 0; a front strip of the slab carries the text 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' in dark brown (#5A3A10). Cylinders stand upright along +Y at x = -3.6, -1.2, +1.2, +3.6, all at z = 0. Each tube: outer radius 0.30, height 6.2, wall glass pale blue-grey #C9DDE6 at ~0.35 opacity with a thin #8FB6C6 outline; flared pour spout at the top flaring from r=0.30 to r=0.48 over the top 0.45 units; hexagonal stepped foot at the bottom, circumradius 0.55, height 0.30, same glass tint. Oil column fills from y=0.35 up to y=5.55 (about 85% of tube), radius 0.27, with a slight meniscus dome at the top. Oil colors (vertical gradient, lighter at top): SAE 20 #F6E0A0 -> #EDC96B; SAE 30 #F2CE63 -> #E8B33F; SAE 40 #F2B45A -> #E8873A; SAE 50 #F07A52 -> #E8432A. Spheres: radius 0.23, polished steel, base #B4B7BA with bright specular highlight upper-left and darker #6E7175 lower-right. Resting (single-instant) sphere heights measured off the source as fraction of the oil column, from column bottom: SAE 20 = 0.26, SAE 30 = 0.38, SAE 40 = 0.52, SAE 50 = 0.68 — i.e. y ≈ 1.70, 2.33, 3.05, 3.89. Grade labels '20', '30', '40', '50' lie flat on the slab top face (or float just above it) centered under each cylinder, dark grey #333, cap height ~0.35. Physics for motion: Stokes terminal velocity v = 2r^2(rho_s - rho_f)g / (9*eta), with eta increasing roughly linearly with grade; use relative viscosities eta(20):eta(30):eta(40):eta(50) = 1.00 : 1.45 : 2.05 : 2.85, giving relative terminal speeds 1.00 : 0.69 : 0.49 : 0.35 so that after a fixed drop time the spheres land at the fractional heights above. Display labels e.g. 12.0, 8.3, 5.9, 4.2 mm/s. For the slider, interpolate viscosity and oil color continuously between the four anchor grades.
interactionPlan.notes: Render glass tubes as double-sided MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission/opacity ~0.3, roughness 0.05, and render oil as a separate slightly smaller inner cylinder with a vertical gradient texture or a custom shader lerping two colors along uv.y — avoids costly refraction. Draw oil before glass with correct depth sorting (transparent: true, renderOrder on glass > oil > sphere) so spheres read as submerged. Spheres use MeshStandardMaterial metalness 0.9, roughness 0.2 with an environment map for the chrome highlight. Text ('Oil viscosity (SAE)', grade numbers, terminal-velocity callouts) via canvas-texture sprites or Troika text; callout labels billboard toward the camera and anchor to each sphere with a short leader line. Animation: integrate position with an exponential approach to terminal velocity (v = v_term * (1 - exp(-t/tau)), tau ~ 0.15 s) so the brief acceleration phase is visible before steady descent; loop with a 1 s pause at the bottom then reset to the top. Slider mode can dim/fade the other three cylinders to 20% opacity rather than removing them. Lighting: one key directional light from upper-left, soft hemisphere fill, and a contact-shadow plane under each hexagonal foot. Camera: mild perspective (fov ~28) nearly front-on and slightly above so the slab top face and the ellipse of each tube mouth are just visible, matching the source.

authoredContext:
The test tubes shown here contain equal amounts of the specified motor oils. Identical metal spheres were dropped at the same time into each of the tubes, and a brief moment later, the spheres had fallen to the heights indicated in the illustration. Rank the motor oils in order of increasing viscosity, and explain your reasoning:

An image of four graduated cylinders sitting on a table labeled “Oil viscosity ( S A E )” is shown. The left-hand cylinder, labeled “20,” is mostly filled with light tan liquid and a metal ball is drawn in the lower fifth of the cylinder, but not on the bottom. The second cylinder, labeled “30,” is mostly filled with light brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn about three-fourths of the way down cylinder. The third cylinder, labeled “40,” is mostly filled with medium brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn halfway down the cylinder. The right-hand cylinder, labeled “50,” is mostly filled with brown liquid and a metal ball is drawn near the top of the liquid in the cylinder.

Viscosity of motor oils

⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Oil colors are heavily desaturated: the source shows a clear yellow → gold → orange → vivid red progression, while the render shows pale beige/tan columns with only a faint pink for SAE 50, so the key visual cue of increasing grade is weak.
The steel spheres are almost invisible — drawn behind a 0.78-opacity oil cylinder they read as faint tan blobs rather than the distinctly bright chrome/grey balls that dominate the source figure.
The '20/30/40/50' grade labels and the 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' caption render very small on the slab, whereas in the source they are large, high-contrast type; hierarchy is lost.
The glass tubes are very transparent and low-contrast against the white background; the source shows crisper blue-grey glass walls, rims and the flared spout outline.
Graduation ticks and a contact shadow/meniscus detail are added that are not present (or barely present) in the source, adding mild visual noise to the tubes.
evaluation.notes: Composition, cylinder/foot/spout geometry, sphere heights and the rich interaction set (drop animation, grade slider, focus mode, terminal-velocity callouts, 4-step guided demo) are all strong and conceptually correct, but washed-out oil colors, nearly invisible steel spheres and undersized slab labels make the render noticeably less recognizable than the source.

feedback.rationale: The concept, interaction set, and geometry are correct; the issues are purely rendering details—washed-out oil colors, low-visibility spheres, and undersized labels—which are generator-level fixes.

plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four tall graduated cylinders arranged side by side on a common base labeled "Oil viscosity (SAE)," each filled with motor oil of a different SAE grade — 20, 30, 40, and 50 from left to right — and each holding a metal sphere dropped simultaneously from the top so that its position at a single elapsed moment reveals the oil's resistance to flow. The oils range progressively in color from pale yellow (SAE 20) to a deeper orange-red (SAE 50), and the position of the sphere descends less and less as the SAE grade increases: the sphere has fallen to the lower portion of the tube in grade 20, slightly higher in grade 30, noticeably higher in grade 40, and only to slightly above the midpoint of the column in grade 50. Because a more viscous fluid exerts a greater drag force on the sphere, slowing it to a lower terminal velocity, the shorter distance traveled in a fixed time directly encodes the ranking of viscosity across grades. The side-by-side format at a single instant converts viscosity — an intrinsic property — into a visually comparable positional difference, removing any need for stopwatches or calculations. This figure demonstrates viscosity as a rank-orderable physical property and establishes that higher SAE-grade oils offer greater internal resistance to the motion of an object moving through them.

elements: Flat rectangular wooden/amber base slab (platform) with visible top face and front edge, spanning the full width of the scene
Text label 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' printed on the front face / front strip of the base slab
Four identical tall graduated cylinders standing upright, evenly spaced left to right on the slab
Each cylinder: transparent pale blue-grey glass tube wall with thin outline
Each cylinder: flared conical pour spout/lip at the top, slightly wider than the tube
Each cylinder: hexagonal stepped glass foot/base at the bottom
Oil column inside each tube filling ~85% of the tube height, with a meniscus at the top surface
Oil color graded by SAE number: pale yellow (20), yellow (30), orange (40), orange-red (50), each with a vertical light-to-dark gradient
One polished steel sphere suspended inside each oil column, with specular highlight and soft shadow
Sphere heights differ: lowest in SAE 20, progressively higher in 30, 40, and highest in 50
Numeric grade labels '20', '30', '40', '50' on the slab top surface directly beneath each cylinder
Soft contact shadows of the cylinder feet on the slab

interactions.label: Drop all four spheres simultaneously
interactions.teaches: At a single elapsed instant, the sphere has fallen farthest in the thinnest oil and least in the thickest, so distance fallen ranks viscosity directly

interactions.label: Oil SAE grade (single-cylinder focus)
interactions.teaches: Viscosity varies continuously: raising the grade darkens the oil and smoothly slows one ball's steady descent

interactions.label: Show terminal velocity labels
interactions.teaches: Each sphere settles at a constant terminal speed inversely proportional to viscosity — the numbers behind the visual ranking
The cylinders are real 3D tubes on a slab; rotating confirms the spheres are inside the fluid columns, not drawn on a flat panel

demo_steps.title: The four oils at rest
demo_steps.narration: Four graduated cylinders hold motor oils of grade SAE 20, 30, 40 and 50, each darkening in color as the grade rises. A steel sphere waits at the top of each column.

demo_steps.title: Release all four at once
demo_steps.narration: Released together, the spheres separate almost immediately: the one in SAE 20 races down while the one in SAE 50 crawls. Distance fallen in the same time ranks the oils' resistance to flow.

demo_steps.title: Read the terminal speeds
demo_steps.narration: Each sphere quickly reaches a constant terminal velocity where drag balances weight. The labels show the speed falling as viscosity climbs from grade 20 to 50.

demo_steps.title: Sweep one cylinder through the grades
demo_steps.narration: Focusing on a single tube and sliding the grade from 20 to 50 shows the change is continuous — the oil deepens toward orange-red and the ball's steady descent slows smoothly.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: base slab 10 x 0.45 x 2.6 world units (X = screen-right width, Y = slab thickness, Z = depth), top face at y = 0; a front strip of the slab carries the text 'Oil viscosity (SAE)' in dark brown (#5A3A10). Cylinders stand upright along +Y at x = -3.6, -1.2, +1.2, +3.6, all at z = 0. Each tube: outer radius 0.30, height 6.2, wall glass pale blue-grey #C9DDE6 at ~0.35 opacity with a thin #8FB6C6 outline; flared pour spout at the top flaring from r=0.30 to r=0.48 over the top 0.45 units; hexagonal stepped foot at the bottom, circumradius 0.55, height 0.30, same glass tint. Oil column fills from y=0.35 up to y=5.55 (about 85% of tube), radius 0.27, with a slight meniscus dome at the top. Oil colors (vertical gradient, lighter at top): SAE 20 #F6E0A0 -> #EDC96B; SAE 30 #F2CE63 -> #E8B33F; SAE 40 #F2B45A -> #E8873A; SAE 50 #F07A52 -> #E8432A. Spheres: radius 0.23, polished steel, base #B4B7BA with bright specular highlight upper-left and darker #6E7175 lower-right. Resting (single-instant) sphere heights measured off the source as fraction of the oil column, from column bottom: SAE 20 = 0.26, SAE 30 = 0.38, SAE 40 = 0.52, SAE 50 = 0.68 — i.e. y ≈ 1.70, 2.33, 3.05, 3.89. Grade labels '20', '30', '40', '50' lie flat on the slab top face (or float just above it) centered under each cylinder, dark grey #333, cap height ~0.35. Physics for motion: Stokes terminal velocity v = 2r^2(rho_s - rho_f)g / (9*eta), with eta increasing roughly linearly with grade; use relative viscosities eta(20):eta(30):eta(40):eta(50) = 1.00 : 1.45 : 2.05 : 2.85, giving relative terminal speeds 1.00 : 0.69 : 0.49 : 0.35 so that after a fixed drop time the spheres land at the fractional heights above. Display labels e.g. 12.0, 8.3, 5.9, 4.2 mm/s. For the slider, interpolate viscosity and oil color continuously between the four anchor grades.
interactionPlan.notes: Render glass tubes as double-sided MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission/opacity ~0.3, roughness 0.05, and render oil as a separate slightly smaller inner cylinder with a vertical gradient texture or a custom shader lerping two colors along uv.y — avoids costly refraction. Draw oil before glass with correct depth sorting (transparent: true, renderOrder on glass > oil > sphere) so spheres read as submerged. Spheres use MeshStandardMaterial metalness 0.9, roughness 0.2 with an environment map for the chrome highlight. Text ('Oil viscosity (SAE)', grade numbers, terminal-velocity callouts) via canvas-texture sprites or Troika text; callout labels billboard toward the camera and anchor to each sphere with a short leader line. Animation: integrate position with an exponential approach to terminal velocity (v = v_term * (1 - exp(-t/tau)), tau ~ 0.15 s) so the brief acceleration phase is visible before steady descent; loop with a 1 s pause at the bottom then reset to the top. Slider mode can dim/fade the other three cylinders to 20% opacity rather than removing them. Lighting: one key directional light from upper-left, soft hemisphere fill, and a contact-shadow plane under each hexagonal foot. Camera: mild perspective (fov ~28) nearly front-on and slightly above so the slab top face and the ellipse of each tube mouth are just visible, matching the source.
